name: Fuel pump
seoDesc: Fuel pump: work out fuel type from the power and the flow rate. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the power, the flow rate, the base fuel pressure and the fuel pump pressure and the Fuel pump calculator solves for fuel type. It suits a practical question that turns up in daily life. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Fuel pump calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fuel pump calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports fuel type in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the induction type and the fuel system type); then you type in the power, the flow rate, the base fuel pressure and the fuel pump pressure.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in metric horsepowers. The unit chip switches it to any of the 21 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as naturally aspirated, turbocharged and supercharged. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in liters per hour. The unit chip switches it to any of the 39 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in bars. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as return and returnless. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in bars. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.

3 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fuel pump calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Fuel type=flow rate ÷ (induction type × power)
Boost pressure=(-base fuel pressure + fuel pump pressure) ÷ fuel system type

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.
  • Shown in bars, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Power, opening in metric horsepowers
  • Flow rate, opening in liters per hour
  • Pressure, opening in bars
  • Pressure, opening in bars
  • Pressure, opening in bars

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fuel pump calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the power, the flow rate and the base fuel pressure — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Fuel pump calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns fuel type, derived from the power, the flow rate and the base fuel pressure. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fuel pump calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the power, the flow rate, the base fuel pressure and the fuel pump pressure, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter power in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Power opens in metric horsepowers and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Fuel pump calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
